title: Chalmers to focus on savings in mini-budget
full_text:
Treasurer Jim Chalmers is preparing a mini-budget of spending cuts and red tape reform as he faces criticism he will impose austerity measures on low-paid Australians while adding to the nation's inflationary pressures.
Chalmers - under political pressure over inflation that has climbed to 4.3 per cent and the Reserve Bank's five interest hikes this year - yesterday revealed the focus of next month's update would be savings.
He said the savings were needed to deal with the "intensifying spending pressures" facing the government, including high interest on debt and the rising costs of essential services, and to deal with inflation.
But the savings package would not put at risk the economy, which Chalmers said was the second-fastest growing of all G7 nations.
"It will cut enough, but not too much. It will strike some fine balances. It will help ease immediate capacity pressures without putting growth at risk," he said.
Greens leader David Shoebridge accused Chalmers and the government of planning deep cuts that would hurt ordinary workers.
"Austerity under Labor is nothing new, but it's particularly brutal right now. There is no justification for the prime minister to make pensioners, people with disabilities and ordinary workers pay for a budget shortfall while leaving billions in potential public revenue on the table," he said.
Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson said the mid-year update had to be a proper mini-budget and not a "touch-up" that delivered net savings in every year across the forward estimates.
"If the treasurer gets this right, inflation comes down, the pressure comes off interest rates, and families and small businesses get the breathing room to get ahead again," he said.
"If he gets it wrong, Australians will keep paying for a cost-of-government crisis through higher prices and higher interest rates for longer."
The last mini-budget was under Paul Keating in the late 1980s, when he put in place tax reforms including deep cuts in then Australia's high tariffs.
This week, the Greens said they were open to examining a proposal from independent MP Allegra Spender to modify the government's capital gains tax plans to axe the current 50 per cent discount and return it to an inflation-adjusted system.
The treasurer has written to Spender to argue her proposal, which includes reducing the discount to 40 per cent and keeping the inflation-adjusted component only for passive assets such as property, could leave innovative firms worse off. He said Treasury analysis suggested it could introduce "pervasive incentives to restructure for tax reasons", as investors would be able to put properties into an "active" business to avoid capital gains tax.
Spender said the treasurer's analysis failed to consider the concerns of businesses, their approach to investment and the real-world impacts on risk-taking.
"My alternative proposal offers greater simplicity, certainty and a more competitive tax regime for risk-taking than the government's [plan] carve-out. That is why so many business people and economists are behind it," she said.
Chalmers revealed the government was planning to build on the $10 billion productivity package outlined in the May budget, with a second package to be developed for next year's fiscal blueprint.
He said this would include an overhaul of the business tax system with a focus on streamlining obligations, using more pre-filled information and automating tax reports and payments.
Public consultation would start on two options. One would be pre-filling contractor income for sole traders in a move Chalmers said would save 400,000 hours of paperwork and around $37 million in costs per year.
A second option would be to simplify elements of the fringe benefits tax reporting system by axing assessments for benefits worth less than $300. Chalmers said this could save businesses about $15 million a year in paperwork costs.
The reduction in red tape is aimed at improving productivity. But research released yesterday by Westpac suggests businesses have started lifting investment in new equipment that will turn around the malaise.
Senior Westpac economist Pat Bustamante said investment in IT, particularly on data centres, had reached its highest share of the economy since the advent of personal computers and the internet in the early 1990s.
There had also been a lift in spending in the energy sector, which had now reached its highest share of GDP since 1983, while investment in the personal services sector is at a record high.
Bustamante said the drag on productivity caused by large spending in non-market parts of the economy such as health and education was coming to an end.
He said productivity growth would probably rise to around 1 per cent or more, which would be stronger than the Reserve Bank's most recent forecast.
